definition: Clemency means mercy shown by someone in power toward a person who has earned a punishment, softening what they deserve.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word clemency. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know clemency should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The judge granted clemency to the first-time offender who had repaid every stolen dollar before sentencing, reducing the term to probation.
Leniency is weaker than clemency — it is everyday mildness, like a teacher grading gently, without the weight of an official act of mercy.
Amnesty is stronger than clemency — it is a sweeping official forgiveness granted to a whole group at once, often erasing offenses entirely.

Mercy is the broad name for kind treatment of someone you have the power to punish — anyone, anywhere, can show mercy. Clemency is mercy in its official form: an act by a judge, governor, or board that deliberately softens a punishment the person genuinely deserves.

Forbearance is self-restraint — patiently holding back from demanding what you are owed or striking back when provoked. Clemency is not restraint but action: someone in power steps in and formally reduces a deserved punishment. You show forbearance by doing nothing; you grant clemency by decree.

Compassion is the sympathy you feel for another person's suffering. It is an emotion, and it may lead to nothing at all. Clemency is what a person in power actually does: the concrete official act of softening a deserved punishment. A judge can feel compassion yet still refuse clemency.

The school board showed clemency to the senior who reported his own grading-system prank, cutting the recommended expulsion to a two-week suspension.
The student really was guilty and really could have been expelled.
The board's decision to soften the punishment out of mercy — while still acknowledging the wrong — is what clemency means.
Clemency flows downward from power — a governor, judge, board, or boss softens a punishment that someone genuinely deserves.
Keep it distinct from its neighbors in this unit: a reprieve merely delays a punishment without reducing it, and vindication proves the person was never to blame at all.
Clemency alone means mercy despite real guilt.

In 1911 a dockworker named Elias Verro was convicted of smuggling and sentenced to nine years — a term even the prosecutor called correct under the law.
The conviction was never in doubt.
Verro had signed a confession, and the appeals court upheld every finding.
What his family sought instead was clemency.
Their petition did not argue innocence; it asked the governor to weigh the man — a first offense, three children, a foreman willing to rehire him — and soften the punishment he deserved.
The governor's counsel reviewed the file for a year.
In the end she commuted the term to the eighteen months already served, while letting the conviction stand.
Editorials approved: the law had spoken, they wrote, and then the state's one merciful office had spoken after it.
